title: Users who run 50+ workflows never churn — should we push everyone to 50?

scenario.role: You're the growth analyst at Cadence
scenario.company: Cadence — a workflow-automation tool with a free tier
scenario.situation: The Head of Product has a striking chart: users who've run 50 or more workflows churn at about 1%, while everyone under 50 churns at 92%. He wants to make '50 workflows' the North Star and push every new user toward it — onboarding nudges, email drips, in-app prompts — on the theory that hitting 50 makes users stick. He'd like you to validate the '50-workflow' target from the data before it goes into the roadmap.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "Users with 50+ workflows basically never churn. If we get every new user to 50 workflows, we'll crush churn."
scenario.question: Does running 50+ workflows actually cause users to stay? Assess whether '50 workflows' is a real lever or a mirage, and recommend what to target instead.

columns.name: engagement_score
columns.description: Underlying engagement propensity (0-100), measured from early behaviour

columns.name: workflows_first_month
columns.description: Workflows the user ran in their FIRST 30 days — available to every user regardless of tenure

columns.name: workflows_total
columns.description: Total workflows the user has run to date (accumulates with tenure)

columns.name: churned
columns.description: 1 if the user has churned, else 0

guidingQuestions: Confirm the headline: churn rate for users with workflows_total ≥ 50 vs < 50.
How long have the 50+ users been around? Compare mean tenure_months for the two groups. Could a brand-new user even reach 50 workflows?
Is workflows_total a cause of retention, or a by-product of it? Which way does the arrow run between 'stayed a long time' and 'ran a lot of workflows'?
Look at workflows_first_month — a signal every user can produce in their first 30 days. How strongly does THAT predict churn, compared with the 50+ total?
What do you tell the Head of Product — is '50 workflows' a lever you can pull on new users, and what's a fairer target?
suggestedApproach: Reproduce the 1%-vs-92% churn split so you know the exact claim.
Ask what it takes to be in the 50+ group. If reaching 50 workflows requires months of use, then churned and new users are excluded by construction — the group is defined by survival.
Separate cause from consequence: total workflows accrue because a user stayed, so 'high total → low churn' is close to circular.
Find a fair signal — one every user can generate early, before tenure differs. Compare how well workflows_first_month predicts churn versus the survivor-defined total.
Recommend a target based on the early, equally-available signal, and note that engagement still confounds even that — the honest test is an experiment.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Users with 50+ total workflows churn at ~1%, versus ~92% for everyone else — a 91-point gap. It looks like the single most powerful retention lever imaginable: get users to 50 workflows and churn all but disappears.
teachingNote.theTrap: Total workflow count is something you can only accumulate by sticking around. The 50+ group has been a customer for ~17 months on average; the under-50 group, ~2.7 months. A user who churns in week two literally cannot run 50 workflows, and a brand-new user hasn't had time to. So 'ran 50+ workflows' is essentially a restatement of 'survived a long time' — the comparison is close to circular. You're not discovering that workflows cause retention; you're measuring the outcome (retention) on the input (workflows) and finding they agree, because one produces the other.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Use a signal every user can generate on a level playing field: activity in the first 30 days, which doesn't depend on tenure. First-month activity does predict churn — high vs low first-month users churn at ~45% vs ~79% — but that gap (33 points) is a fraction of the survivor-defined 91-point gap, and even it largely reflects underlying engagement rather than a causal effect of the activity itself. '50 total workflows' is not a lever you can pull on a new user: you can't manufacture the total without the months of retention that create it. Target early activation and engagement, and prove any 'do X to retain' claim with an experiment, not a threshold that only survivors can clear.
howToGetThere: Compute churn for workflows_total ≥ 50 (~1%) vs < 50 (~92%). The 91-point gap should look too good to be true.
Check tenure by group: ~17 months vs ~2.7. Reaching 50 workflows requires time the churned/new users never had — that's the survivorship tell.
Reason about direction: total workflows is downstream of retention, so conditioning on it selects survivors.
Switch to a fair, tenure-independent signal — workflows_first_month — and compare churn for high vs low (~45% vs ~79%, a 33-point gap).
Note even that is confounded by engagement; conclude the '50-workflow' target is a mirage and recommend an activation experiment.
teachingNote.lesson: Beware any metric that can only be reached by surviving — cumulative usage, tenure milestones, lifetime totals. Splitting on it compares survivors to everyone else, so it will always look like a miracle retention driver even when it causes nothing. The number is measuring the outcome you care about, not a cause of it. To find a real lever, use signals available to every user at the same point in their lifecycle, and confirm cause with an experiment rather than a threshold that only the retained can clear.
